newsitem.title: MEXICO: Real funds rate little help for Fed policy - Jordan.
newsitem.headline: Real funds rate little help for Fed policy - Jordan.

text.p: The inflation-adjusted real federal funds rate is of little help as a guideline for U.S. monetary policy because it is difficult to pinpoint at any given time, Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland President Jerry Jordan said.

"Real interest rates, like real money suppy, are theoretical concepts that are difficult to use in real-time policy making because they are like unicorns," Jordan told Reuters. "They exist in theory, we know what they look like, but we never get to observe them."

Jordan spoke to Reuters in an interview conducted after a monetary policy conference held November 27-December 1. The conference was hosted by a business grouping, Instituto Mexicano de Ejecutivos de Finanzas (IMEF).

Fed officials have cited the zero, inflation-adjusted real funds rate as one of the reasons for launching a preemptive tightening cycle in 1994 when the benchmark U.S. overnight interbank lending rate, then at 3.0 percent, was barely matching the inflation rate.
The funds rate has been at 5.25 percent since January 31, and core inflation is running at 2.6 percent.
Jordan pointed out productivity measurement as one of the issues most debated at the Fed in the current environment of healthy growth, job creation and low inflation.

"All the great industrial revolutions have not only challenged policy makers, but they have challenged statisticians to accurately record what is actually going on," Jordan said, in reference to the computer-driven technology revolution taking place in the service-heavy U.S. economy.
"When two-thirds of the U.S. economy was agriculture and manufacturing, we talked about cycles, with crops' failures and things wearing out," Jordan added.
"In an information age, and with today's communications and virtually everything coming in the form of services, we don't have that anymore," the Cleveland Fed president also said.
Jordan said the services-based Gross Domestic Product is hard to accurately measure, meaning productivity measurements are imprecise.

"It's a contributing factor to my thinking," said Jordan, a voting member of the Federal Open Market Committee who did not dissent this year against the Committee's decision to keep rates steady despite high levels of resource utilization.
Accuracy in measuring productivity is important because it allows for estimates about whether nominal GDP growth reflects inflationary pressures and requires a tighter monetary stance.

Jordan, in a speech on Saturday before the IMEF, said "evidence consistently points to a negative correlation between inflation and the growth of productivity over the post-Korean War period in the United States."

In a separate interview with Reuters, Jordan also made the point that a successful anti-inflation monetary policy has allowed the U.S. unemployment rate to drop to levels that economists would have deemed inflationary in the past.

"The central bank must provide the highest possible incentives for the creation and accumulation of wealth and that, above all else, means they must provide a stable monetary system," Jordan said, reiterating a point made in his speech.
